worldBrief:
# The world on 1 October 1962

**The superpowers.** Seventeen years after Hiroshima, the United States and the Soviet Union face each other across a divided world. America holds a large lead in deliverable nuclear weapons: some 200 ICBMs, Polaris submarines and a huge bomber force against a few dozen Soviet ICBMs. Kennedy, stung by the Bay of Pigs (April 1961) and the Vienna summit, has expanded conventional forces and runs Operation Mongoose, a CIA sabotage campaign against Castro. Congressional midterm elections are due on 6 November and Republicans attack the administration over Cuba.

**Cuba.** Castro has declared himself a Marxist-Leninist. The OAS excluded Cuba in January and the US has imposed a near-total embargo since February. Since July, Soviet ships have been arriving in unusual numbers. U-2 flights in August and September photographed SA-2 surface-to-air missile sites, MiG-21 fighters, coastal-defence cruise missiles and Komar missile boats. Moscow insists all of it is defensive. On 4 and 13 September Kennedy warned that "the gravest issues would arise" if offensive weapons appeared in Cuba, and Congress is completing a joint resolution authorising force if necessary. U-2 overflights of western Cuba have been restricted since early September for fear of the SAMs.

**Berlin and Germany.** The Berlin Wall has stood since 13 August 1961. Khrushchev still demands a German peace treaty that would end Western rights in West Berlin, and threatens to sign a separate treaty with Ulbricht. Adenauer, now 86, is building a special partnership with de Gaulle, who toured West Germany in triumph in September. (On this map, West Berlin lies inside the East German province of Brandenburg.)

**Europe.** Western Europe is booming. The six-member Common Market is working, and Britain, Denmark, Ireland and Norway have applied to join. Britain's negotiations in Brussels are stuck over Commonwealth trade and agriculture, and de Gaulle is sceptical. France has just ended the Algerian war (Évian accords, March; independence, 5 July). The settler terrorist OAS nearly killed de Gaulle at Petit-Clamart on 22 August; he has called a referendum for 28 October on direct presidential elections. Albania has sided with China and stopped taking part in the Warsaw Pact and COMECON. Tito's Yugoslavia is non-aligned.

**The communist schism.** The Sino-Soviet split is now open. Soviet experts left China in 1960 and the two parties trade polemics. China is recovering from the Great Leap Forward famine, which killed tens of millions. Along the Himalayan border, India's "forward policy" has placed posts in territory China claims. There have been clashes in Ladakh and, since 8 September, Chinese troops have pressed on Indian positions below the Thag La ridge in the North-East Frontier Agency. Nehru does not believe China will start a major war.

**Southeast Asia.** The Geneva agreement of 23 July 1962 neutralised Laos under a coalition led by Souvanna Phouma, but the Pathet Lao and North Vietnamese troops remain and the Ho Chi Minh Trail runs through the country. In South Vietnam the Viet Cong insurgency is growing. Diem's government relies on strategic hamlets and some 9,000 American advisers, while helicopter units fly ARVN troops into combat. In August the Netherlands agreed to hand West New Guinea to Indonesia. The UN Temporary Executive Authority (UNTEA) takes over today, 1 October, and Indonesia gets the territory on 1 May 1963. This scenario keeps it Dutch until then. Britain plans to merge Malaya, Singapore, North Borneo and Sarawak into Malaysia by August 1963. Sukarno and the Philippines (which claims Sabah) object.

**Middle East.** On 26 September army officers under Abdullah al-Sallal overthrew Imam al-Badr, who had succeeded his father only a week earlier, and proclaimed the Yemen Arab Republic. The Imam escaped to the northern mountains, where Saudi Arabia and Jordan back royalist tribes. Nasser has promised military support, and the first Egyptian troops are on their way. Syria broke away from the United Arab Republic in September 1961, although Egypt keeps the name. Iraq's Qasim claims Kuwait and is fighting a Kurdish revolt led by Mustafa Barzani. Israel faces hostile neighbours along the 1949 armistice lines. Jordan holds the West Bank and Egypt administers Gaza.

**Africa.** Decolonisation is sweeping the continent. Seventeen states became independent in 1960. Since then Sierra Leone, Tanganyika, Rwanda, Burundi and Algeria have followed, and Uganda follows on 9 October. Britain still rules Kenya, Zanzibar, the High Commission Territories, Gambia and Aden. The Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland is crumbling: Britain has accepted that Nyasaland may secede. In the Congo, Katanga's secession under Tshombe continues despite UN forces and the U Thant reunification plan of August. Portugal is fighting a rebellion in Angola that began in 1961 and refuses to decolonise. South Africa has left the Commonwealth, banned the ANC and holds South West Africa. Nelson Mandela was arrested in August.

**Latin America.** In Argentina, the military overthrew Frondizi in March and its factions fought in the streets in September. Peru has been under a junta since July. Brazil's Goulart rules under a parliamentary system imposed to limit him. Venezuela's Betancourt faces leftist guerrillas and put down two military revolts in May and June. The Dominican Republic heads for its first free election since Trujillo's assassination.

**The space race and technology.** Glenn orbited the Earth in February; in August the Soviets flew two Vostok capsules at once. On 12 September Kennedy pledged to reach the Moon. Both sides have tested nuclear weapons in the atmosphere throughout 1962.
rules:
# Simulation rules: Cold War (October 1962)

**Realism first.** Outcomes follow how the world worked in 1962. A single turn rarely changes much. Big shifts need sustained effort, allies and luck.

**Nuclear brinkmanship.** The United States, the Soviet Union, Britain and France have nuclear weapons. China is working on a bomb. America's strategic lead is large but cannot prevent catastrophic damage to itself or Europe. Leaders bluff, threaten and probe, and confrontations move up a ladder: warnings, alerts, blockades, mobilisation. Both sides fear miscalculation. An attack on a superpower's forces or on a protected ally risks escalation that no rational leader wants. Any nuclear use is a world-changing catastrophe with immense casualties and political consequences.

**Two blocs and the non-aligned.** NATO and the Warsaw Pact face each other in Germany. Bloc members follow their leader on core security questions, though de Gaulle, Romania and others seek more room. Moscow will use force to keep Eastern Europe in line, as in Hungary in 1956. Washington backs friendly dictators against communist movements and will intervene, openly or covertly, in its hemisphere. The non-aligned states play the superpowers against each other for aid and arms, and their votes decide the UN General Assembly.

**The communist schism.** The Sino-Soviet split is real and deepening. China and the Soviet Union compete for the loyalty of communist parties, liberation movements and the Third World. Albania sides with Beijing, while North Korea and North Vietnam balance between the two.

**Decolonisation.** The empires are being wound up. Britain negotiates independence colony by colony and usually transfers power peacefully, except where settlers resist (Kenya, the Rhodesias). Portugal and South Africa fight to hold on. New states are fragile: coups, secessions, army mutinies and one-party rule are common, and the superpowers court them with aid. When a colony gains independence, the colonial power's provinces there pass to a new state.

**Proxy wars and insurgency.** Guerrilla wars (Vietnam, Laos, Angola, Yemen, the Congo) are slow and politically costly. Conventional armies struggle against insurgents who have sanctuaries and outside support. Superpowers prefer advisers, arms and covert action to sending combat troops.

**Wars are costly.** Mid-century armies can move fast against weak opponents, but wars between serious powers are bloody and draw in allies. War exhaustion rises, economies suffer and outside powers resupply the weaker side.

**Limited information.** There is no internet and no satellite television news. Intelligence comes from spies, diplomats, radio intercepts, U-2 flights and early reconnaissance satellites. It is slow, partial and often wrong. Governments can keep secrets for weeks, deny deployments, and are surprised by events. Communications between capitals take hours, and there is no hotline between Washington and Moscow. Leaders can misread each other's intentions.

**Economics.** The Bretton Woods system of fixed exchange rates and the dollar anchors the West. Western Europe and Japan are growing fast, the Soviet bloc grows through central planning, and much of the Third World depends on commodity exports. Trade between the blocs is small and controlled (CoCom). Embargoes hurt small targets like Cuba badly but do little to the Soviet Union.

**Domestic politics matter.** Democracies hold scheduled elections and suffer scandals and strikes. Military coups are a normal way to change government in Latin America, Africa, the Middle East and Asia. Communist leaders face Politburo intrigue rather than voters. Racial segregation in the US South and apartheid in South Africa shape both domestic and international politics.

**Diplomacy and institutions.** The UN Security Council is paralysed by vetoes on Cold War issues. The Republic of China holds China's seat. The General Assembly is a stage for anti-colonial majorities. NATO decisions need consensus. Summits are rare, formal events.

**Plausibility.** Countries act according to their interests, capabilities and leaders' personalities. Surprises happen, such as coups, assassinations, defections, uprisings and accidents, but they should be rooted in existing tensions. Avoid hindsight: no one in 1962 knows how the Cold War will end.

formables.name: Reunified Germany
formables.concept: The two German states reunited under one government, ending the division of Europe's heartland.

formables.name: United Korea
formables.concept: Peaceful or forced reunification of the Korean peninsula under one government.

formables.name: Reunified Vietnam
formables.concept: One Vietnam from the Chinese border to the Mekong delta, as the 1954 Geneva accords once promised through elections.

formables.name: Maphilindo
formables.concept: A confederation of the Malay peoples of Malaya, the Philippines and Indonesia (Macapagal's proposal).

formables.name: Federation of Malaysia
formables.concept: Malaya federated with Singapore, North Borneo (Sabah) and Sarawak, as planned in London for 1963.

formables.name: Expanded United Arab Republic
formables.concept: Nasser's union revived and enlarged: Egypt, Syria and the new Yemeni republic under one flag.

formables.name: Pan-Arab Union
formables.concept: A single Arab state from the Atlantic to the Gulf, the dream of Nasserists and Ba'athists alike.

formables.name: Arab Federation
formables.concept: The Hashemite union of Iraq and Jordan (1958), restored as a counterweight to Nasser.

formables.name: Union of African States
formables.concept: The Ghana-Guinea-Mali union turned into a real federation, the nucleus of Nkrumah's United States of Africa.

formables.name: Greater Somalia
formables.concept: All Somali-inhabited lands united: Somalia plus the Ogaden (Ethiopia), Kenya's Northern Frontier District and French Somaliland.

formables.name: West Indies Federation
formables.concept: Revival of the British Caribbean federation dissolved in May 1962, with Jamaica, Trinidad and the smaller islands.

formables.name: Central African Federation
formables.concept: The Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland preserved and recast, or extended, as a multiracial dominion.

formables.name: East African Federation
formables.concept: Tanganyika, Kenya, Uganda and Zanzibar federated, as Nyerere proposed (he offered to delay independence for it).

formables.name: Balkan Federation
formables.concept: Tito's old plan of a socialist federation of Yugoslavia, Bulgaria and Albania.

formables.name: Nordic Union
formables.concept: A Scandinavian defence and economic union, as discussed in 1948-49.
